en: The Sūtra on the Merit of Counting Beads Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Ratnaciṃtā of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, desiring to benefit...
For the benefit of all sentient beings, with a heart of great compassion, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Listen well! I shall now expound the distinctions in the benefits and the comparative merit of receiving, maintaining, and using rosaries."

If there are those who recite various dhāraṇīs and the names of the Buddhas, desiring to benefit themselves and protect others, and seeking to swiftly attain the realization of all dharmas, their method for using the rosary should be as follows; it must be maintained and observed.
If one uses iron for the rosary, reciting and counting one round yields fivefold merit;
if one uses red copper for the rosary, reciting and counting one round yields tenfold merit;
if one uses pearls, coral, and the like for the rosary, reciting and counting one round yields a hundredfold merit.

If one uses *kṣauma* seeds as a rosary, for every single recitation and bead-counting, one obtains a thousandfold merit; if one seeks rebirth in the pure lands of the Buddhas or the celestial palaces, one should receive this rosary.
If one uses lotus seeds as a rosary, for every single recitation and bead-counting, one obtains ten-thousandfold merit;
if one uses *indrākṣa* beads as a rosary, for every single recitation and bead-counting, one obtains a millionfold merit.
If one uses *ulūṭarakhāśa* as a rosary, for every single recitation and bead-counting, one obtains ten million times the merit;
if one uses crystal as a rosary, for every single recitation and bead-counting, one obtains ten billion times the merit;

if one uses bodhi seeds as a rosary—whether counting and reciting with them or merely holding them in hand—the merit from each recitation is immeasurable, beyond calculation, and difficult to compare.
"O sons of good family!

As for the bodhi-jujube seed (bodhi-phala), if there is a person who holds this bead in their hand but cannot recite the names of the Buddhas or dharanis according to the ritual, yet this son of good family merely carries it with them while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—whatever words they utter, whether good or evil—by virtue of this person holding the bodhi-jujube seed, the merit obtained shall be equal to that of reciting the names of all Buddhas and chanting mantras; there is no difference, and they will obtain immeasurable merit."
Regarding the rosary, it must consist of exactly one hundred and eight beads.

If these are difficult to obtain, one may instead use fifty-four, twenty-seven, or even fourteen; all of these are acceptable for use. This constitutes the distinctions in the characteristics of the rosary.
“O sons of noble family!
For what reason do I now alone praise the use of bodhi-fruit seeds as yielding the most supreme benefit?
Listen well, all of you, and I shall recount for you once more the causes from the past.”
In the past, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world and attained perfect enlightenment beneath this very tree.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner who, holding false and inverted views, slandered the Triple Gem. He had a son who was suddenly struck and killed by a non-human spirit.
The non-Buddhists thought to themselves:
"Our heterodox views are now flourishing; we do not yet know what supernatural powers the Buddhas possess.
Since the Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment beneath this tree, if the Buddha is truly a sage, the tree should manifest a response."
He then laid his deceased son beneath the Bodhi tree and spoke these words:
"If this Buddha-tree is holy, my son shall surely revive.
After reciting the name of the Buddha for seven days, the son regained consciousness once more.
The non-Buddhists praised him, saying:
"We have never before seen the supernatural power of the Buddhas.
That the Buddha has manifested such a rare wonder beneath the tree of enlightenment is a matter of immense majesty and virtue, truly inconceivable."
All the non-Buddhists and others abandoned their heterodox ways to return to the Right Path, gave rise to the bodhicitta, and came to believe that the power of the Buddha is inconceivable.
All people thereafter called it the Tree of Prolonging Life.
"For these reasons, it has two names; you should know this.
Having spoken these words for you all to see what was necessary," the Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī Dharma Prince! It is exactly as you have said;
there is not the slightest difference.”
When the entire great assembly heard this exposition on the merit of counting beads, they were all filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Thus ends the *Buddhabhāṣita-mālā-guṇa-parīkṣā-sūtra*.
